children: By Jeanne Whalen

Fresh off big state-level election wins, Democrats around the country are pushing ahead with pledges to combat the high cost of living. They are also facing new budget strains worsened by federal cuts.

States with new or strengthened Democratic trifectas — or control of both statehouse chambers and the governor's office — have the most ambitious plans. They include subsidizing child care and housing construction, expanding tax credits for parents and other caregivers, using state funds to forgive medical debt, and offering free meals to more students.

They have some wind in their sails: State finances have improved in recent years, boosted by stronger economic growth, federal pandemic stimulus funds and rising sales- and income-tax collections, according to S&P Global analyst Oscar Padilla. But federal cuts to Medicaid, food assistance and other programs are beginning to clobber state budgets, with the cuts set to soar in the coming years.

"In the background of many individuals expecting Democrats to expand affordability initiatives, I have to remind folks that we have to keep the lights on," said Sarah Anthony, a Democrat who chairs Michigan's Senate Appropriations Committee.
Come January, Democrats will hold a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010 and unified control of two dozen state legislatures. They will add six trifectas, for a total of 22.

In Minnesota, Democrats want to flex their newfound muscle by offering new healthcare tax credits. In Wisconsin, they are eyeing free school meals for every child and property tax relief. And in Pennsylvania, they want to invest state funds in housing construction.

Medicaid cuts from the tax and spending bill President Trump signed last year have been slowly ramping up, but 90% of the cuts are still to come, in fiscal years 2029 to 2034, according to a report from S&P Global Ratings. Those cuts, along with reduced funding for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, are already forcing states to tighten their belts, the report said.
"Shifting federal policy dynamics could narrow states' funding options to balance budgets while they execute large-scale investments that aim to address cost-of-living pressures," the report said.

Still, in Michigan, Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson has ambitious plans for after she is sworn in on Jan. 1. Backed by a newly reclaimed trifecta, she aims to pass a $5,000 tax credit for caregivers, expand medical-debt relief and widen access to child care and preventive healthcare. Benson also wants to guarantee teachers a minimum starting salary of $60,000 a year.

Michigan is facing about a $700 million budget deficit for the coming 2028 fiscal year, partly driven by federal funding cuts, according to Bob Schneider, a budget and tax policy expert at the Citizens Research Council of Michigan. The state may end up with higher-than-expected revenue this year from corporate income-tax collections, which would help close that gap, he said. But major new financial commitments to fund affordability programs would require new taxes or spending cuts elsewhere, he said.
Benson has said she won't raise taxes on the middle class, and that she will bolster revenue by closing tax loopholes, driving economic growth and making government more efficient.

Anthony, the state senator, said her priority is maintaining programs Michigan has already adopted to improve affordability — including an expanded earned-income tax credit and free school meals — though she added that voters have demanded "bigger and bolder" assistance.

"New revenue would be the only way to truly deliver new sweeping affordability measures," she said. Down the road, some Democrats want to scrap the state's flat income tax in favor of a graduated system with higher rates on top earners, though that would require voter approval through a ballot measure.

Colorado voters just did exactly that, replacing a flat income tax with one that imposes higher rates on people and businesses making more than $500,000 a year. The new levy is expected to generate at least $2 billion in extra revenue annually, which by law must be spent on healthcare, child care and education.

The funds will more than close the $1 billion budget deficit Colorado had been facing in the coming fiscal year, Democratic Rep. Emily Sirota, chair of the state legislature's Joint Budget Committee, said in an interview. But given how quickly the state's Medicaid costs are growing — just as federal Medicaid funding is falling — it isn't clear how much of the extra funds will be available to finance anything beyond Medicaid, she added.

"My personal goal is to ensure we are doing something transformational with these dollars," said Sirota, who won an election that will soon send her to the Colorado Senate. There is "a tremendous opportunity to make investments in our child care program," she said, while noting a state commission is working on proposals to rein in Medicaid spending growth.

Democratic Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, meanwhile, is promising to expand down-payment assistance for first-time home buyers, lower the cost of college and expand universal preschool. Democrats already had a trifecta in Colorado but gained supermajorities in both chambers of the legislature.

In Nevada, the Democratic Gov.-elect Aaron Ford unseated the Republican incumbent Joe Lombardo, giving Democrats a trifecta. Ford has pledged to expand programs that help renters cover security deposits, utility payments and rent, and increase funding for down-payment assistance for first-time home buyers. He also aims to invest in community health centers and mobile clinics.

At the same time, Ford has acknowledged the threats from federal cuts to Medicaid, which insures about a quarter of Nevadans. His campaign site pledged to work with state agencies "to mitigate the impact for Nevadans who will lose coverage."
